questions.stem: Soup cools according to \(\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-21)\), where k is positive. Initially \(T(0)=96^circ C\). Show that \(T=21+75e^{-kt}\) is a solution.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Differentiating gives \(dT/dt=-75ke^{-kt}\). Also \(-k(T-21)=-k(75e^{-kt})=-75ke^{-kt}\), so the proposed function satisfies the differential equation. At t=0, \(T=21+75=96\), so it also satisfies the initial condition.
questions.hint: Differentiate the proposed temperature function and separately substitute it into the right side of the differential equation.

keyPoints.note: Differentiate the exponential term using the chain rule.
Check the initial condition after checking the differential equation.

Both sides agree, and the initial value is correct.

questions.stem: \(N\) is the number of finches in a certain population at time \(t\) years. The population size \(N\) satisfies the equation \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=-k(N-1500)\), for some constant \(k\). Verify that \(N=1500+Ae^{-kt}\) (where \(A\) is a constant) is a solution of the equation \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=-k(N-1500)\). Which working correctly verifies this?
questions.hint: Differentiate \(N=1500+Ae^{-kt}\) (the derivative of the constant 1500 is 0), then rewrite \(Ae^{-kt}\) as \(N-1500\).

steps.explain: Start with the proposed solution and differentiate with respect to \(t\). The derivative of a constant (1500) is 0, and \(\dfrac{d}{dt}e^{-kt}=-ke^{-kt}\) (chain rule: multiply by the derivative \(-k\) of the power).
Now express the right-hand side of the differential equation. From \(N=1500+Ae^{-kt}\), subtract 1500: \(N-1500=Ae^{-kt}\).
Substitute \(Ae^{-kt}=N-1500\) into the derivative.
This is exactly the given equation, so \(N=1500+Ae^{-kt}\) is a solution for any constant \(A\) ✓.
Why not the others: B has the wrong sign (the derivative of \(e^{-kt}\) is NEGATIVE); C replaces \(Ae^{-kt}\) by \(N\) instead of \(N-1500\); D thinks the derivative of 1500 is 1500 (it is 0).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Differentiate, then replace A e to the minus kt by N minus 1500.

questions.stem: A quantity \(N\) has an initial value of 900 and the rate of change of \(N\) is given by the equation \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=0.35(N-500)\). Which graph shows the relationship between \(N\) and \(t\)?
questions.hint: Do not solve fully: ask (1) what is \(N\) at \(t=0\)? (2) is \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}\) positive or negative there? (3) where is \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=0\) (the dotted line)? The sign of \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}\) tells you whether the graph rises or falls.

steps.explain: Find the equilibrium (where nothing changes): \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=0\) when \(N-500=0\). So the line \(N=500\) is special (dotted in the graphs).
Starting value: \(N(0)=900\) is ABOVE 500, so \(N-500=400>0\). Then \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=0.35\times400=140>0\): the quantity is INCREASING at \(t=0\).
As \(N\) gets bigger, \(N-500\) gets bigger, so \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}\) gets bigger: it grows faster and faster (exponential growth AWAY from 500; the curve bends UP and never comes back).
Check with the general solution of \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=k(N-c)\): \(N=c+Ae^{kt}\). Here \(c=500\), \(k=0.35>0\), and \(N(0)=900\) gives \(A=400\).

So the graph starts at 900 (above the dotted line 500), increases and curves upward. Only D does this. A starts at 400 and falls; B starts at 900 but FALLS toward 500 (that would need \(k<0\)); C starts at 500 (not 900).
So the correct choice is option D.

keyPoints.text: Which graph shows the relationship between \(N\) and \(t\)?
keyPoints.note: \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=0\) at \(N=500\); \(N(0)\) above it with \(k>0\) grows.

questions.hint: Look for where the direction segments are horizontal (slope 0), then where they are vertical (undefined).

keyPoints.note: A horizontal short segment indicates \(dy/dx=0\); vertical segments indicate an undefined slope.

steps.explain: In the supplied field, horizontal segments lie along the diagonal through the origin with positive gradient about 2. That means the numerator must vanish when \(y=2x\).
The near-vertical segments occur on the line \(2y-x=0\), so this expression belongs in the denominator.
Combine the numerator and denominator identified from the field.

questions.hint: Check where the slopes are horizontal and where the slope changes sign.

steps.explain: Look at simple places first. Along the \(y\)-axis (\(x=0\)) the segments are horizontal, so \(\frac{dy}{dx}=0\) when \(x=0\). That rules out B and D (they are undefined at \(x=0\)).
Next compare signs. At \((2,1)\) the slope is positive, but at \((2,-1)\) (below the \(x\)-axis) it is negative. So the sign of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) changes when \(y\) changes sign.

steps.explain: Find where the segments are vertical: along \(y=x\). There \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) is undefined, so the denominator is \(x-y\) or \(y-x\).
Decide the sign with one point, e.g. \((1,0)\) on the positive \(x\)-axis, where the slope is positive (segments go up to the right).
So the equation is \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x+y}{x-y}\), option A.

keyPoints.text: Which of the following could be the differential equation represented?
keyPoints.note: Slope 0 along y = −x and vertical along y = x; test (1, 0) for the sign.

questions.hint: The direction field gives the gradient \(\dfrac{dV}{dt}\) at each point. Look at (1) the SIGN of the slopes, (2) what happens at \(V=0\), and (3) how the slopes change as \(V\) increases.

steps.explain: Sign: every slope mark leans downwards to the right, so \(\dfrac{dV}{dt}<0\) for all \(V>0\). Options C and D are positive (for \(k>0\)), so reject them.
At \(V=0\) the marks are horizontal (gradient 0), and as \(V\) increases the marks become steeper and steeper (more negative).
Test option B: \(-\dfrac{k}{V}\) is undefined at \(V=0\), and it becomes LESS steep as \(V\) increases, the opposite of the diagram. Reject.
Test option A: \(-kV^{2}\) is 0 at \(V=0\) and gets more negative as \(V\) grows (e.g. \(V=10\) is 100 times steeper than \(V=1\)). This matches the diagram.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Slopes negative, zero at V = 0, and steeper as V grows.

meta.source: Frensham School 2021 Year 12 Trial HSC Examination Mathematics Extension 1

questions.stem: The spread of flu through a student population is modelled by the equation \(S=\dfrac{2000}{1+199e^{-0.4t}}\) where \(S\) is the total number of students infected after \(t\) days. The slope field of \(\dfrac{dS}{dt}=\dfrac{S}{5}\left(2-\dfrac{S}{1000}\right)\) is shown. There are 3 regions labelled \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) in which a solution curve can be found. In which one of these three regions can the solution curve exist? Justify your answer with reference to constant solutions and the initial value of \(S\).

options: Region \(B\): \(\dfrac{dS}{dt}=0\) at \(S=0\) and \(S=2000\) (constant solutions, horizontal slope lines), and solution curves cannot cross them. \(S(0)=\dfrac{2000}{1+199}=10\) lies between 0 and 2000, so the curve stays in Region \(B\).
Region \(A\): as \(t\to\infty\), \(S\to2000\), so the curve must lie above the constant solution \(S=2000\).
Region \(C\): as \(t\to-\infty\), \(S\to0\), so the curve must lie below the constant solution \(S=0\).
Any region: a solution curve can cross a constant solution, so it can start in \(B\) and later enter \(A\).
questions.hint: Constant solutions are where \(\dfrac{dS}{dt}=0\): \(S=0\) and \(S=2000\). Solution curves NEVER cross them. Find \(S(0)\) from the formula to see which region it starts in.

steps.explain: Constant solutions: \(\dfrac{dS}{dt}=0\iff\dfrac{S}{5}\left(2-\dfrac{S}{1000}\right)=0\iff S=0\) or \(S=2000\). These are the horizontal slope lines (red dashed), which separate the regions.

steps.explain: Initial value: put \(t=0\) in \(S=\dfrac{2000}{1+199e^{-0.4t}}\).

\(0<10<2000\), so the starting point is in Region \(B\) (green point). A solution curve cannot cross a constant solution (uniqueness), so it stays between \(S=0\) and \(S=2000\) for ever: as \(t\to\infty\), \(S\to2000\) from below; as \(t\to-\infty\), \(S\to0\) from above.
Why not the others: A would need \(S(0)>2000\); C would need \(S(0)<0\); D is false because solution curves cannot cross constant solutions.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: In which one of these three regions can the solution curve exist
keyPoints.note: Starting value 10 is between the constant solutions 0 and 2000, and curves cannot cross them.

steps.explain: Read the field. In the 1st and 3rd quadrants the line segments slope DOWNWARDS (negative gradient); in the 2nd and 4th quadrants they slope UPWARDS (positive gradient). On the \(x\)-axis the segments are horizontal (gradient 0); on the \(y\)-axis they are vertical (gradient undefined).

Why not the others: \(\dfrac{y}{x}\) and \(\dfrac{x}{y}\) would give POSITIVE gradients in Q1 and Q3; \(-\dfrac{x}{y}\) is horizontal on the \(y\)-axis and vertical on the \(x\)-axis (the opposite of the picture).
So the correct choice is option C.

questions.stem: Solve \(\frac{dy}{dx}=y^2\cos x\), given \(y(\pi/6)=-\frac{1}{2}\).
questions.hint: Separate the y and x terms, integrate, and use the initial condition to find the constant.

keyPoints.note: Move (1/y^2) beside dy and (\cos x) beside dx.
Use this value after integrating to determine the constant.

steps.explain: Separate variables.
Integrate both sides.
Substitute \(x=\pi/6, y=-1/2\).
Rearrange for y.

questions.stem: Find the particular solutions to the differential equation \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2x-1}{y^2}\) given \(y=\sqrt[3]{3}\) when \(x=0\).
questions.hint: Separate: ∫y² dy = ∫(2x − 1) dx, then find c from the initial value.

steps.explain: Separate the variables.
Solve for \(y\).

keyPoints.note: Separate variables, integrate, then substitute x = 0, y = ∛3 to find c.

questions.stem: A solution to the differential equation \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{\cos(x+y)+\cos(x-y)}\) can be obtained from:
questions.hint: Expand cos(x + y) + cos(x − y) = 2cos x cos y, then separate.

steps.explain: Expand both cosines with the compound angle formulas.
steps.work: \(\cos(x+y)+\cos(x-y)=(\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y)+(\cos x\cos y+\sin x\sin y)=2\cos x\cos y\)

steps.explain: Simplify the differential equation.
Separate the variables: multiply by \(\cos y\) and by \(dx\).
Integrate both sides: option A.

keyPoints.note: The denominator simplifies to 2cos x cos y; then separate variables.

questions.stem: Solve \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y^2}{1+x^2}\) given \(y(0)=1\).
questions.hint: Separate: ∫y⁻² dy = ∫dx/(1 + x²). Remember ∫y⁻² dy = −1/y.

steps.explain: Separate the variables.
Integrate both sides.
Solve for \(y\).
Check: at \(x=0\), \(y=1\) ✓. Missing the minus sign from \(\int y^{-2}dy=-y^{-1}\) gives option B.

keyPoints.note: Separate variables, integrate, then use y = 1 at x = 0 to find c.

questions.stem: Solve the differential equation \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{(2-y)\sqrt{2-x^2}}\) given that when \(x=1\), \(y=0\). Express \(y\) as a function of \(x\).
questions.hint: Separate, use the initial condition, complete the square in y, choose the sign using y(1) = 0.

steps.explain: Separate the variables.
Multiply by \(-2\) and complete the square in \(y\).
\(y-2=\pm\sqrt{\dots}\). At \(x=1\), \(y=0\) so \(y-2=-2\lt0\): take the negative root.
Check at \(x=1\): \(\sqrt{\frac\pi2+4-\frac\pi2}=2\), so \(y=0\) ✓.

keyPoints.note: After integrating, complete the square in y; y(1) = 0 decides the ± sign.

questions.stem: At time \(t\) seconds the length of the side of a cube is \(x\) cm, the surface area of the cube is \(S\) cm², and the volume of the cube is \(V\) cm³. The surface area of the cube is increasing at a constant rate of \(8\,\text{cm}^2\text{s}^{-1}\).
questions.hint: Connect the changing cube dimensions to S and V first. For the final part, solve the resulting separable differential equation and apply its initial condition.

keyPoints.note: This gives the value of \(dS/dt\).
Use \(S=6x^2\) for a cube.
Use \(V=x^3\) to connect volume and side length.

parts.stem: Show that \(\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{k}{x}\) where k is a constant.
parts.answer: \(S=6x², so dS/dt=12x(dx/dt)=8 and dx/dt=2/(3x); hence k=2/3.\)
parts.hint: Write the cube’s surface area in terms of x, differentiate with respect to time, and use dS/dt=8.

keyPoints.note: Focus on this information from the question when choosing the method and carrying out the calculation.

steps.explain: A cube has six square faces, each of area x².
Differentiate with respect to t using the chain rule because x varies with time.
Insert the stated surface-area rate.
Divide by 12x and identify k.

parts.hint: Use V=x³ and substitute the rate dx/dt found in the previous part.

keyPoints.note: Focus on this information from the question when choosing the method and carrying out the calculation.

steps.explain: Write the cube volume in terms of its side.
Differentiate with respect to time.
Substitute dx/dt=2/(3x) and simplify.
Replace x with V^(1/3), since V=x³.

parts.stem: Given that \(V=8\) when \(t=0\), solve the differential equation in part (b), and find the value of \(t\) when \(V=16\sqrt2\).
parts.hint: Separate the variables in dV/dt=2V^(1/3), integrate both sides, then use V(0)=8.

keyPoints.note: Use this initial condition after integrating to determine the constant.
Substitute this into the integrated equation and simplify its power first.

steps.explain: Separate variables.
Integrate both sides.
Use V=8 at t=0 to find C.
Rearrange to isolate V^(2/3).
Evaluate the target volume's power.
Solve and state time units.

questions.stem: For the differential equation \(y′=\frac{6}{5x^2+4x-1}\):
questions.hint: Factor the denominator, separate the partial fractions, integrate, and then apply the given point.

keyPoints.note: Focus on this information from the question when choosing the method and carrying out the calculation.

parts.stem: For the differential equation \(y′=\frac{6}{5x^2+4x-1}\), show that \(y′=\frac5{5x-1}-\frac1{x+1}\).
parts.hint: Factor the denominator, then combine the proposed partial fractions over a common denominator to verify the numerator is 6.

keyPoints.note: Focus on this information from the question when choosing the method and carrying out the calculation.

steps.explain: Factor the denominator.
Combine the proposed partial fractions over the common denominator.
Expand the numerator; the x terms cancel.
This reproduces the original derivative, proving the decomposition.

parts.stem: Find the solution to the differential equation, given that when \(x=\frac12\), \(y=3\).
parts.hint: Integrate the partial fractions, include the constant, then use the initial condition to determine it.

keyPoints.note: Focus on this information from the question when choosing the method and carrying out the calculation.

steps.explain: Integrate each term in the decomposition.
For the first term, u=5x−1 and du=5dx; integrate the second logarithm directly.
Combine logs and add the integration constant.
Substitute x=1/2,y=3 to determine C.
On the interval containing x=1/2, x>1/5 and the ratio is positive.

questions.stem: Consider the differential equation: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3x^2+4}{2y}\). Find a solution to the equation in the form \(y=f(x)\), given that \(f(2)=1\).
questions.hint: Separate the variables: \(2y\,dy=(3x^2+4)\,dx\), integrate both sides, then use the point to find the constant.

steps.explain: Separate.
Integrate both sides.
Solve for \(y\) (positive root since \(f(2)=1>0\)).

keyPoints.note: Separate the variables and integrate.

questions.stem: For the differential equation \(y'=\dfrac{6}{5x^{2}+4x-1}\): Show that \(y'=\dfrac{5}{5x-1}-\dfrac{1}{x+1}\). Which working is correct?
questions.hint: Combine the two fractions over a COMMON denominator \((5x-1)(x+1)\): cross-multiply the numerators. Be careful with the minus sign in front of the second numerator, then expand the denominator to see it matches \(5x^{2}+4x-1\).

steps.explain: Common denominator: \((5x-1)(x+1)\). Multiply the first numerator by \((x+1)\) and the second by \((5x-1)\).
Expand the numerator, being careful with the minus sign: \(-1(5x-1)=-5x+1\).
Expand the denominator: \((5x-1)(x+1)=5x^{2}+5x-x-1=5x^{2}+4x-1\).
Why not the others: B has a sign error (\(-(5x-1)=-5x+1\), not \(-5x-1\)); C adds/subtracts denominators (not allowed); D uses wrong cross-multiplication.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Common denominator; watch the minus sign.

questions.stem: For the differential equation \(y'=\dfrac{6}{5x^{2}+4x-1}\): Find the solution to the differential equation, given that when \(x=\dfrac{1}{2}\), \(y=3\).
questions.hint: Use the partial fractions from the previous part: \(y'=\dfrac{5}{5x-1}-\dfrac{1}{x+1}\). Integrate each term (\(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'}{f}=\ln|f|\)), combine the logs, then use the point \(\left(\dfrac{1}{2},3\right)\) to find the constant.

steps.explain: Integrate. Since \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(5x-1)=5\), the first term is already \(\dfrac{f'}{f}\); the second is \(\dfrac{1}{x+1}\).
Combine the logarithms: \(\ln a-\ln b=\ln\dfrac{a}{b}\).
Use \(x=\dfrac{1}{2}\), \(y=3\): the fraction \(\dfrac{5\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-1}{\frac{1}{2}+1}=\dfrac{\frac{3}{2}}{\frac{3}{2}}=1\) and \(\ln1=0\).
Write the solution.
Why not the others: B combines with a PRODUCT (the second term is subtracted); C forgets the constant \(+3\); D has a coefficient 5 on the first log (the 5 is already used by \(\dfrac{f'}{f}\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

parts.hint: Combine the right-hand side over the common denominator.

Simplify the numerator.

questions.stem:
A team of biologists released 500 fish into a lake with a maximum carrying capacity of 10000 fish. It was found that the number of fish tripled during the first year. The fish population, \(N\), in the lake after \(t\) years is modelled by the logistic equation:

\(\frac{dN}{dt}=kN(10000-N)\)

where \(k\) is a constant.

parts.stem: Given \(\frac{10000}{N(10000-N)}=\frac1N+\frac{1}{10000-N}\), solve the differential equation to show that the fish population after \(t\) years is \(N=\frac{10000}{1+19e^{-10000kt}}\).
parts.hint: Separate variables, integrate with the given partial fractions, use N = 500 at t = 0.

steps.explain: Separate the variables and multiply both sides by 10000.
Integrate from \(t=0\) (\(N=500\)) using the given partial fractions.
Combine the logs and substitute the lower limit: \(\frac{500}{9500}=\frac{1}{19}\).
Flip the fraction (negate the log) and exponentiate.
Solve for \(N\).

keyPoints.note: Separate variables; the given partial fractions make the N-integral two logs.

steps.explain: The population tripled in the first year: \(N=3\times500=1500\) at \(t=1\).
Rearrange.
Take logs.

parts.answer: Tripled in the first year: N = 1500 at t = 1. \(1500=\frac{10000}{1+19e^{-10000k}}\Rightarrow1+19e^{-10000k}=\frac{20}{3}\Rightarrow e^{-10000k}=\frac{17}{57}\Rightarrow k=\frac{1}{10000}\ln\frac{57}{17}\).

keyPoints.note: Use N = 1500 (three times 500) at t = 1.

parts.stem: Correct to the nearest month, how long will it take for the fish population in the lake to reach 7000 fish?
parts.hint: Use e^(−10000k) = 17/57, set N = 7000 and solve for t, then convert years to months.

steps.explain: Take logs.
Convert to months.

questions.stem: The spread of flu through a student population is modelled by the equation \(S=\dfrac{2000}{1+199e^{-0.4t}}\) where \(S\) is the total number of students infected after \(t\) days. Show that the given equation for \(S\) satisfies the differential equation \(\dfrac{dS}{dt}=\dfrac{S}{5}\left(2-\dfrac{S}{1000}\right)\). Which working is correct?
options: \(\dfrac{dS}{dt}=\dfrac{2000\cdot199e^{-0.4t}}{1+199e^{-0.4t}}\) (differentiating the top only), and substituting \(S\) gives \(\dfrac{S}{5}\left(2-\dfrac{S}{1000}\right)\).
\(\dfrac{dS}{dt}=\dfrac{2000(0.4)(199)e^{-0.4t}}{\left(1+199e^{-0.4t}\right)^{2}}\), which is already equal to \(\dfrac{S}{5}\left(2-\dfrac{S}{1000}\right)\), so no further working is needed.
questions.hint: Differentiate with the chain rule (write \(S=2000(1+199e^{-0.4t})^{-1}\)). Then express everything in terms of \(S\): from \(S(1+199e^{-0.4t})=2000\) you get \(1+199e^{-0.4t}=\dfrac{2000}{S}\).

steps.explain: Rewrite as a power so the chain rule is easy.
Differentiate: bring down \(-1\), reduce the power to \(-2\), multiply by the derivative of the inside \(199\cdot(-0.4)e^{-0.4t}\). The two negatives give a positive.
Split the fraction: one factor \(\dfrac{2000}{1+199e^{-0.4t}}=S\) and the other \(\dfrac{0.4\cdot199e^{-0.4t}}{1+199e^{-0.4t}}\).

Simplify: \(0.4\cdot\dfrac{S}{2000}\cdot\left(\dfrac{2000}{S}-1\right)=0.4\left(1-\dfrac{S}{2000}\right)\), so \(\dfrac{dS}{dt}=0.4S\left(1-\dfrac{S}{2000}\right)=\dfrac{2S}{5}-\dfrac{S^{2}}{5000}=\dfrac{S}{5}\left(2-\dfrac{S}{1000}\right)\).
Why not the others: B differentiates only the numerator; C stops without rewriting in terms of \(S\); D has a sign error (the derivative is positive).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Chain rule, then replace the exponential with S using S(1 + 199e) = 2000.

questions.stem: The spread of flu through a student population is modelled by the equation \(S=\dfrac{2000}{1+199e^{-0.4t}}\) where \(S\) is the total number of students infected after \(t\) days. According to this model, after how many days does the rate of increase reach a maximum? Give your answer to the nearest number of days.
questions.hint: The rate of increase is \(\dfrac{dS}{dt}=\dfrac{S}{5}\left(2-\dfrac{S}{1000}\right)\), a downward parabola in \(S\) (it is a quadratic in \(S\) with negative \(S^{2}\) coefficient). It is greatest at the vertex \(S=-\dfrac{b}{2a}\). Then find \(t\) from the formula for \(S\).

steps.explain: Expand: \(\dfrac{dS}{dt}=-\dfrac{1}{5000}S^{2}+\dfrac{2}{5}S\). This is a parabola in \(S\) with \(a<0\) (concave down), so the maximum is at the vertex.
Vertex: \(S=-\dfrac{b}{2a}\).
The rate is greatest when \(S=1000\) (half of the limit 2000; the steepest point of the logistic curve, the point of inflection). Find the time: \(1000=\dfrac{2000}{1+199e^{-0.4t}}\).
To the nearest day: 13 days.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: after how many days does the rate of increase reach a maximum
keyPoints.note: Rate is a downward parabola in S; maximum at S = 1000, then solve for t.

questions.stem: In a group of 1000 computers linked to each other via the internet, the number \(N\) infected with a virus at time \(t\) years is given by \(N=\dfrac{1000}{1+ce^{-1000t}}\) where \(c\) is a constant. Show that, eventually, all the computers will be infected with the virus. Which statement is correct?
options: As \(t\to\infty\), \(e^{-1000t}\to\infty\), so \(N\to\dfrac{1000}{\infty}=0\): none of the computers
questions.hint: 'Eventually' means as \(t\to\infty\) (a very long time). Look at what happens to \(e^{-1000t}\) when \(t\) is huge: a NEGATIVE exponent, so the term shrinks to 0.

steps.explain: 'Eventually' = after a very long time: let \(t\to\infty\).
The exponent \(-1000t\) becomes very negative, and \(e^{\text{very negative}}\) is tiny (like \(\dfrac{1}{e^{1000t}}\)).
Substitute into the formula.
The total number of computers is 1000, so eventually ALL are infected (the graph levels off at the red line \(N=1000\)).
Why not the others: B reverses the direction of \(e^{-1000t}\); C is about \(t=0\), not 'eventually'; D invents a limit for the bracket.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Show that, eventually, all the computers will be infected with the virus.
keyPoints.note: Eventually means \(t\to\infty\): \(e^{-1000t}\to0\).

questions.stem: In a group of 1000 computers linked to each other via the internet, the number \(N\) infected with a virus at time \(t\) years is given by \(N=\dfrac{1000}{1+ce^{-1000t}}\) where \(c\) is a constant. Show that \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=N(1000-N)\). Which working is correct?
questions.hint: Two sides to compare. Left: differentiate \(N=1000(1+ce^{-1000t})^{-1}\) with the chain rule. Right: simplify \(N(1000-N)\) (the term \(1000-N\) needs a common denominator). Show both equal \(\dfrac{10^{6}ce^{-1000t}}{(1+ce^{-1000t})^{2}}\).

steps.explain: Write \(N\) as a negative power so the chain rule can be used. Let \(u=1+ce^{-1000t}\).
Differentiate: \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=1000(-1)u^{-2}\dfrac{du}{dt}\).
Right side: first find \(1000-N\) using the common denominator \(u\).
Multiply by \(N=\dfrac{1000}{u}\).
Both sides equal the same expression, so \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=N(1000-N)\) (the logistic equation: growth is fastest when \(N=500\)).
Why not the others: B forgets the chain rule (the derivative of \(e^{-1000t}\)); C loses the minus signs (\(-1\times-1000\) is POSITIVE); D only simplifies the right side.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Chain rule gives \(\dfrac{10^{6}ce^{-1000t}}{u^{2}}\); so does \(N(1000-N)\).

questions.stem: Soup cools according to \(T=21+75e^{-kt}\), where t is minutes after removal from the stove. It is 87°C after 5 minutes. How much longer after that measurement must Miriam wait for it to reach 70°C?
questions.hint: Use the 87°C measurement to find k; then solve for the total time when T=70°C and subtract 5 minutes.

keyPoints.note: Substitute this measurement to determine the cooling constant k.
Find the total time to 70°C, then subtract the 5 minutes already elapsed.

steps.explain: Use \(T(5)=87\) to find k.
Solve the model for the total time when T=70.
Subtract the first five minutes already elapsed.

questions.stem:
Metal Fatigue is a phenomenon where a piece of steel will fail when repeatedly subjected to force \(F\). The endurance limit is the force below which the steel will not break even if subjected to an infinite number of application of that force. Let the number of applications be \(n\).

The force and the number of applications are related by the differential equation \(\frac{dF}{dn}=-k(F-F_0)\) where \(k\) and \(F_0\) are constants.

parts.stem: Show that \(F=275e^{-k(n-1)}+F_0\) is a solution to the differential equation.
parts.hint: Differentiate and replace 275e^(−k(n−1)) by F − F₀.

steps.explain: Differentiate with respect to \(n\).
From the given \(F\), \(275e^{-k(n-1)}=F-F_0\).

keyPoints.note: Differentiate F with respect to n and write the result in terms of F.

parts.stem: If \(F=350\) when \(n=1\), find the value of \(F_0\).

steps.explain: At \(n=1\) the exponent is 0.

keyPoints.note: Substitute n = 1: e^(−k·0) = 1.

parts.stem: Find the exact value of \(k\) if \(F=80\) when \(n=200\).

steps.explain: Substitute with \(F_0=75\).
Take logs.

keyPoints.note: n = 200 gives exponent −k(199). Use F₀ = 75.

steps.explain: The endurance limit is what \(F\) approaches as \(n\to\infty\). Since \(k\gt0\), \(e^{-k(n-1)}\to0\).

keyPoints.note: As n → ∞ the exponential term vanishes.

questions.stem: A piece of hot metal is placed in a room with a surrounding air temperature of 15°C and allowed to cool. It loses heat according to Newton's law of cooling: \(\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-A)\), where \(T\) is the temperature of the metal in degrees Celsius at time \(t\) minutes, \(A\) is the surrounding air temperature and \(k\) is a positive constant. After 5 minutes the temperature of the metal is 75°C, and after a further 3 minutes it is 45°C. Solve the differential equation, expressing your answer in the form \(T=f(t)\) and giving all constants in exact form.
questions.hint: The solution of Newton's law is \(T=A+Ce^{-kt}\) with \(A=15\). Use the two data points to find \(C\) and \(k\).

steps.explain: General solution with \(A=15\).
Divide the equations to find \(k\).
Find \(C\).
Substitute.

keyPoints.note: General solution \(T=A+Ce^{-kt}\), then use the two readings.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the number of pelicans, \(P(t)\), on an island at time \(t\) (the graph starts at 3000 and levels off towards 1500). Which equation best represents this graph?
questions.hint: Check two things in each equation: the value at \(t=0\) (use \(e^{0}=1\)) and the limit as \(t\to\infty\) (use \(e^{-kt}\to 0\)).

steps.explain: Read the graph: it starts at \(P=3000\) when \(t=0\), and it decreases towards the dashed line \(P=1500\) but never reaches it (a horizontal asymptote).

questions.stem: \(N\) is the number of finches at time \(t\) years, with \(N=1500+2000e^{-kt}\) and \(k=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{20}{13}\right)\approx 0.2154\). How long will it take for the population to drop to 2100, correct to one decimal place?
questions.hint: Substitute \(N=2100\), isolate \(e^{-kt}\), then take the natural log and divide by \(-k\).

steps.explain: Subtract 1500, then divide by 2000: \(\dfrac{600}{2000}=0.3\).
Take natural logs: \(\ln e^{-kt}=-kt\).
Solve for \(t\): divide by \(-k\). Use the exact value \(k=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\dfrac{20}{13}\).
Calculate and round to 1 decimal place.

questions.stem: A piece of hot metal is placed in a room with a surrounding air temperature of \(15^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) and is allowed to cool. It loses heat according to Newton’s Law of Cooling: \(\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-A)\) where \(T\) is the temperature of the metal in \({}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), at time \(t\) minutes, \(A\) is the surrounding air temperature and \(k\) is a positive constant. After 5 minutes the temperature of the metal is \(75^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) and after a FURTHER 3 minutes the temperature of the metal is \(45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). What is the value of \(k\) in the above equation?
questions.hint: Solve the cooling equation: \(T=A+Me^{-kt}\). The excess temperature \(T-15\) decays exponentially. Use the two readings, 5 and 8 minutes after the start (5 + a further 3). Divide the two equations to eliminate \(M\).

steps.explain: Separate variables with \(A=15\): \(\dfrac{dT}{T-15}=-k\,dt\). Integrate and rewrite (\(T>15\), so no absolute value needed).
Times: the first reading is at \(t=5\); the second is a FURTHER 3 minutes later, so \(t=5+3=8\) (not 3).
Substitute and subtract 15.
Divide (1) by (2): \(M\) cancels and \(\dfrac{e^{-5k}}{e^{-8k}}=e^{3k}\).
Take natural logs and divide by 3.
Check: \(k>0\) as required (\(\ln0.5<0\) would give a negative \(k\), so A and C are impossible).
So the correct choice is option D.

keyPoints.note: Excess temperature T − 15 decays exponentially; divide the two equations.

questions.stem: A certain chemical treatment of blue-green algae in a river causes it to decrease based on the equation \(A=A_{0}\times e^{kt}\), where \(A\) is the kilograms of algae and \(t\) is time in months. If 250 kg of blue-green algae reduces to 150 kg after 3 months, find how long it will take, to the nearest month, to reduce the blue-green algae to 10 kg.
questions.hint: Step 1: \(A_{0}=250\) (the starting amount). Step 2: use \(A=150\) at \(t=3\) to find \(k\) (it will be NEGATIVE: decay). Step 3: solve \(250e^{kt}=10\) for \(t\).

steps.explain: Take natural logs and divide by 3.
Solve for \(t\) (the two negatives cancel).
To the nearest month: 19 months. Check: \(250e^{-0.1703\times19}=250\times0.0393=9.8\approx10\) ✓. Option B truncates 18.9 instead of rounding.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: find how long it will take
keyPoints.note: Find k from 250 to 150 in 3 months, then solve 250 e to the kt = 10.

questions.stem: A tank contains 2,500 litres of water and 25 kg of dissolved salt. Fresh water enters the tank at a rate of 20 litres per minute. The solution is thoroughly mixed at all times and is drained from the tank at a rate of 15 litres per minute. Using \(y\) for the amount of salt in the tank in kilograms (as a function of time), and \(t\) for time in minutes, show that the concentration of salt in the tank at time \(t\) can be given by \(C=\dfrac{y}{2500+5t}\). Which explanation is correct?
options: Volume at time \(t\) \(=2500+20t-15t=2500+5t\) litres; concentration \(=\dfrac{\text{amount of salt}}{\text{volume}}=\dfrac{y}{2500+5t}\)
The volume stays at 2500 litres, so \(C=\dfrac{y}{2500}\)
questions.hint: Concentration \(=\dfrac{\text{amount of salt (kg)}}{\text{volume of liquid (L)}}\). Find the volume at time \(t\): start volume + water IN − liquid OUT.

steps.explain: Water in: \(20\) litres per minute for \(t\) minutes \(=20t\). Liquid out: \(15\) litres per minute \(=15t\).

Concentration (kg per litre) \(=\) salt \(\div\) volume.
Why not the others: B ignores the net inflow; C ADDS the outflow; D ignores the outflow.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: A tank contains 2,500 litres of water and 25 kg of dissolved salt. Fresh water enters the tank at a rate of 20 litres per minute. The solution is thoroughly mixed at all times and is drained from the tank at a rate of 15 litres per minute. Explain why the rate of change of salt in the tank can be given by \(y'=-15C\). Which explanation is correct?
options: Salt leaves only through the drain: \(15\) litres per minute each carrying \(C\) kg per litre, so the salt leaves at \(15C\) kg per minute; fresh water brings in no salt. So \(y'=-15C\)
Salt enters at \(20\) litres per minute, so \(y'=20C\)
The salt leaves at \(20-15=5\) litres per minute, so \(y'=-5C\)
The salt is constant at 25 kg, so \(y'=0\)
questions.hint: Rate of change of salt \(=\) rate salt comes IN \(-\) rate salt goes OUT. Rate of salt \(=\) (concentration in kg per litre) \(\times\) (litres per minute).

steps.explain: Salt IN: the entering water is FRESH (contains no salt), so salt comes in at 0 kg per minute.
Salt OUT: the drained liquid has concentration \(C\) kg/L and leaves at 15 L/min.
Net rate of change (in minus out) \(=0-15C\).
Why not the others: B uses the inflow rate (but fresh water has no salt); C uses the net change of VOLUME; D ignores the drain (salt is being removed).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Explain why the rate of change of salt in the tank can be given by
keyPoints.note: Salt out = concentration × litres per minute.

questions.stem: A tank contains 2,500 litres of water and 25 kg of dissolved salt. Fresh water enters the tank at a rate of 20 litres per minute. The solution is thoroughly mixed at all times and is drained from the tank at a rate of 15 litres per minute. Find \(y\), the amount of salt in the tank as a function of \(t\).
questions.hint: Combine \(y'=-15C\) and \(C=\dfrac{y}{2500+5t}\) to get a SEPARABLE differential equation: \(\dfrac{dy}{dt}=-\dfrac{15y}{2500+5t}\). Separate the variables, integrate both sides, use \(y(0)=25\).

steps.explain: Substitute \(C\) into \(y'=-15C\).
Separate variables: \(y\) terms on the left, \(t\) terms on the right.
Integrate both sides: \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{15}{2500+5t}dt=3\ln|2500+5t|\) (the \(5\) from the chain rule cancels part of the 15).
Exponentiate: \(y=A(2500+5t)^{-3}\) where \(A=e^{c}\).
Why not the others: B has the wrong power (2 instead of 3); C is exponential decay (it ignores the growing volume); D is upside down (the salt would increase).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Find \(y\), the amount of salt in the tank as a function of \(t\)
keyPoints.note: Separate variables; power comes from 15 ÷ 5 = 3.

questions.stem: A tank contains 2,500 litres of water and 25 kg of dissolved salt. Fresh water enters the tank at a rate of 20 litres per minute. The solution is thoroughly mixed at all times and is drained from the tank at a rate of 15 litres per minute. If the tank has a capacity of 5,000 litres, how much salt is in the tank when it overflows?
questions.hint: Find the TIME when the volume \(2500+5t\) reaches 5000 litres, then substitute that time into the salt formula \(y=\dfrac{25\times2500^{3}}{(2500+5t)^{3}}\).

steps.explain: The tank overflows when the volume reaches its capacity.
At this time the volume in the denominator is 5000 litres (exactly double the starting 2500).
Simplify: \(\dfrac{2500}{5000}=\dfrac{1}{2}\).
Why not the others: \(6.25\) uses the square \(\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\); \(12.5\) uses the first power; 25 is the starting amount.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: how much salt is in the tank when it overflows
keyPoints.note: Overflow at volume 5000: t = 500.

questions.stem: A salad, which is initially at a temperature of \(25^{\circ}\text{C}\), is placed in a refrigerator that has a constant temperature of \(3^{\circ}\text{C}\). The cooling rate of the salad is proportional to the difference between the temperature in the refrigerator and the temperature, \(T\), of the salad. That is, \(T\) satisfies the equation \(\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-3)\), where \(t\) is the number of minutes after the salad is placed in the refrigerator. Show that \(T=3+Ae^{-kt}\) satisfies this equation. Which working is correct?
questions.hint: Differentiate \(T=3+Ae^{-kt}\) with respect to \(t\) (the 3 is a constant, \(A\) and \(k\) are constants), then rewrite \(Ae^{-kt}\) using \(T-3=Ae^{-kt}\).

steps.explain: Differentiate: the derivative of the constant 3 is 0; \(\dfrac{d}{dt}e^{-kt}=-ke^{-kt}\) (chain rule).
From \(T=3+Ae^{-kt}\) we get \(Ae^{-kt}=T-3\).
Substitute \(Ae^{-kt}=T-3\).
Why not the others: B forgets the chain-rule factor \(-k\); C has an extra \(t\); D has the wrong sign (that would be heating).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Differentiate; the chain rule gives −k.

questions.stem: A salad, initially at \(25^{\circ}\text{C}\), is placed in a refrigerator at a constant \(3^{\circ}\text{C}\), where \(T=3+Ae^{-kt}\) (\(t\) in minutes). The temperature of the salad is \(11^{\circ}\text{C}\) after \(10\) minutes. Find the temperature of the salad after \(15\) minutes.
questions.hint: Two unknown constants \(A\) and \(k\), so use two pieces of information: \(T(0)=25\) gives \(A\); \(T(10)=11\) gives \(k\). Then substitute \(t=15\).

steps.explain: Find \(A\) from the initial temperature: \(t=0\), \(T=25\) (\(e^{0}=1\)).
Take natural logarithms of both sides.
Substitute \(t=15\) (keep \(k\) exact on the calculator).
Round to 1 decimal place.
Why not the others: \(4.8\) forgets the \(+3\) (uses \(22e^{-kt}\)); \(8.5\) uses \(A=25\); \(16.3\) uses \(t=5\) instead of 15.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: Find the temperature of the salad after \(15\) minutes
keyPoints.note: Find A from t = 0, then k from t = 10.

questions.stem: In a group of 1000 computers linked to each other via the internet, the number \(N\) infected with a virus at time \(t\) years is given by \(N=\dfrac{1000}{1+ce^{-1000t}}\) where \(c\) is a constant. At the beginning, only one computer was infected with the virus. After how many days will the 50% of the computers be infected?
questions.hint: Step 1: find \(c\) using the start \((t=0,\ N=1)\). Step 2: set \(N=500\) (50% of 1000) and solve for \(t\) using logarithms. Step 3: convert \(t\) from YEARS to DAYS (\(\times365\)).

steps.explain: At the beginning \(t=0\), \(N=1\). Note \(e^{0}=1\).
50% of the computers: \(N=500\).
Solve: multiply by the bracket and divide by 500.
Take natural logs of both sides.
The question asks for DAYS: \(t\) is in years, so multiply by 365.
Why not the others: 6.91 forgets to divide by 1000 (it is \(\ln999\)); 0.0069 is in YEARS; 920 days uses \(\dfrac{1}{999}\) wrongly.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: After how many days will the 50% of the computers be infected?
keyPoints.note: Find \(c\) from \(N(0)=1\); \(N=500\); convert years to days.
